concepts.title: Build squares and find square roots
concepts.text: A square number counts dots in equal rows and columns. A square root asks how many dots are in one row. The principal square root is non-negative, even though both signs can solve a square equation.

concepts.title: Build cubes and find cube roots
concepts.text: A cube has three equal edge lengths. A cube number counts small cubes in equal layers. A cube root undoes cubing; a negative number has a negative real cube root.

concepts.title: Prime groups and perfect powers
concepts.text: For a perfect square every prime occurs in pairs. For a perfect cube every prime occurs in triples. To complete a square or cube, supply only the missing prime factors.

concepts.title: Use a square model in a real situation
concepts.text: Area uses square units; side length uses ordinary units. Read whether a question asks for area, edge or number of objects. Check by squaring or cubing the proposed root.

concepts.text: Multiplication joins lists of equal factors. Division cancels equal factors, provided the denominator is non-zero. A power raised to a power multiplies the exponents.

concepts.title: Zero and negative exponents
concepts.text: Descending powers divide by the base at every step. The zero power of a non-zero base is 1. A negative exponent means reciprocal; it does not mean a negative value.

concepts.title: Powers of ten in measurements
concepts.text: Scientific notation uses a number from 1 up to, but not including, 10. Large quantities have positive powers of ten; tiny quantities have negative powers. Track units and the number of decimal moves.

concepts.title: Why place value matters
concepts.text: The same digit has different values in different positions. A place-value system needs a placeholder for an empty place. Zero represents no units in a place; it is not always removable.

concepts.title: Compare ways to write numbers
concepts.text: An additive numeral adds the values of its symbols. A positional numeral uses both a symbol and its location. We can compare systems without claiming one historical method works exactly like another. Egyptian numerals used repeated powers-of-ten symbols; Roman notation also uses subtractive pairs such as IV. Babylonian place value grouped in base 60; Mayan positional notation commonly grouped in base 20 and used a zero sign. Indian decimal positional notation made ten-place grouping and zero especially powerful. These systems developed over long periods and have different conventions.

concepts.title: Group in bases
concepts.text: Base ten groups ten units into the next place. In base two, digits can only be 0 and 1, and places are powers of 2. Always state the base when a representation could be ambiguous.

concepts.title: Explain a representation
concepts.text: Read from the highest place to the lowest. Multiply each digit by its place value, then add. Use a reverse conversion to check your answer.

concepts.title: Definitions and starting assumptions
concepts.text: A definition gives a word a precise meaning. Axioms are accepted starting statements, not results proved from themselves. A theorem needs a logical argument from accepted facts.

concepts.title: Euclid’s first four postulates
concepts.text: A straight segment can join any two points. A segment can be extended indefinitely; a circle can be drawn with any centre and positive radius. All right angles are equal.

concepts.title: Parallelism and the fifth postulate
concepts.text: The fifth postulate concerns when two lines meet, using interior angles and a transversal. In Euclidean geometry an equivalent statement gives one parallel through a point outside a line. A diagram alone cannot prove two lines never meet.

concepts.title: Justify a construction

concepts.title: Rays, angles and a full turn
concepts.text: A ray has a starting point and continues in one direction. An angle measures a turn between two rays, not the ray lengths. A straight turn is 180 degrees and a complete turn is 360 degrees.

concepts.title: Linear pairs and vertical angles
concepts.text: Adjacent angles forming a straight line are a linear pair. Their sum is 180 degrees. Vertically opposite angles are equal because each supplements the same adjacent angle.

concepts.title: Parallel lines and a transversal
concepts.text: Corresponding and alternate interior angles are equal for parallel lines. Interior angles on the same side of the transversal are supplementary. The converses can establish parallelism if the needed angle relation is given.

concepts.title: Build a short proof
concepts.text: Mark given parallel arrows and identify exact angle pairs. State a reason for every equality. In a triangle, a parallel through a vertex explains the 180-degree angle sum.

concepts.title: Parallelogram properties and their converses
concepts.text: Opposite sides of a parallelogram are parallel and equal. Opposite angles are equal; adjacent angles sum to 180 degrees. Diagonals bisect each other; equal diagonals are a special rectangle property.

concepts.title: The midpoint theorem
concepts.text: The segment joining midpoints of two triangle sides is parallel to the third side. Its length is half the third side. The converse lets a parallel through one midpoint identify the other midpoint.

concepts.title: Medians, centroids and central symmetry
concepts.text: A median joins a vertex to the opposite side’s midpoint. The three medians meet at the centroid, which divides each in ratio 2:1 from the vertex. A parallelogram has half-turn symmetry about the diagonal intersection.

concepts.title: Midpoint quadrilaterals and tiling
concepts.text: Joining side midpoints of any simple quadrilateral produces a parallelogram. The midpoint theorem makes opposite sides parallel to the same diagonal. Half-turn copies of a quadrilateral can form a plane tiling without gaps.

concepts.text: A circle is the set of points at a fixed distance from a centre. A chord joins two boundary points; a diameter is a chord through the centre. The perpendicular from the centre to a chord bisects that chord.

concepts.title: Equal chords and circumcircles
concepts.text: Equal chords of the same or congruent circles have equal distances from their centres. The perpendicular bisectors of a triangle sides meet at its circumcentre. A non-collinear triple has a unique circumcircle.

concepts.title: Angles on the same arc
concepts.text: An angle at the centre is twice an angle at the circumference subtending the same arc. Angles in the same segment are equal. An angle in a semicircle is right; distinguish the arc under consideration.

concepts.title: Cyclic quadrilaterals
concepts.text: A cyclic quadrilateral has all four vertices on one circle. Its opposite angles are supplementary. The converse lets a180-degree opposite-angle sum prove cyclicity for a convex quadrilateral.

concepts.text: A cylinder curved surface unfolds to a rectangle. A cone uses slant height for curved area, but vertical height for volume. A cone has one third the volume of a cylinder with the same base and height.

concepts.title: Spheres, hemispheres and pyramids
concepts.text: A sphere surface has no flat face. A hemisphere total area includes its circular base. A pyramid volume is one third base area times perpendicular height; sloping faces need their own heights.

concepts.title: Recasting, scale and litres
concepts.text: Recasting preserves volume when no material is lost. Doubling lengths multiplies area by 4 and volume by 8. Capacity uses internal dimensions; one litre is 1000 cubic centimetres.

concepts.title: Read and organise data
concepts.text: A frequency counts how often a value or category occurs. Check axis labels, units and total sample size before comparing graphs. A bar graph uses separated categories; a histogram represents contiguous numerical intervals.

concepts.title: Mean, median and mode
concepts.text: The mean uses every value. The median is the middle of sorted observations. The mode is a most frequent value; there may be more than one or no unique mode.

concepts.title: Weighted averages
concepts.text: A combined average must account for group sizes. Multiply each group average by its count to recover its total. For arbitrary group means, directly averaging them is guaranteed correct when group sizes are equal. Otherwise use weights; identical group means are a special case.

concepts.title: Stacked and 100-percent bars
concepts.text: A stacked bar shows the total and its component parts. A100-percent stacked bar shows composition, not absolute size. Compare counts using a common scale and compare percentages with stated totals.

concepts.title: Outcomes, events and equally likely cases
concepts.text: A sample space lists possible outcomes. An event is a collection of outcomes. Counting favourable outcomes works directly only when the listed outcomes are equally likely.

concepts.title: Experimental probability
concepts.text: Relative frequency is an experimental estimate, not an exact prediction. More trials often stabilise an estimate but do not guarantee any exact next outcome. A fair coin can produce uneven short runs.

concepts.title: Use tables and trees
concepts.text: For two ordered coin tosses, HH,HT,TH,TT are distinct equally likely outcomes. Tree branches organise multi-step possibilities. State replacement and independence before multiplying branch probabilities.

concepts.title: Complements and careful interpretation
concepts.text: A probability lies from 0 to 1. A complementary event contains every outcome outside the event. Probability zero means impossible in a finite equally likely model, not merely unlikely.
